title: Signal Hunters Field Scratchpad
content:
Purpose:
This is a personal scratchpad for lightweight, opportunistic few-shot prompt probes aimed at surfacing weak/rare signals in model outputs (hallucinated facts, boundary-case interpretations, inconsistent persona behavior). The idea: fast iterate on tiny exemplar sets and framing heuristics, log failure clusters, and keep a growing library of compact templates for downstream eval harnesses.

Hypotheses I'm chasing (quick list):
- Small curation of edge-case exemplars reduces hallucination of lesser-known entities if anchored with a short source-signal.
- Asking the model to "explain its uncertainty" (one-sentence justification) surfaces spurious certainty and lets us filter outputs.
- Mixing one positive exemplar + one adversarial negative (contrast pair) increases robustness to brittle instruction-following.

Constraints / environment notes:
- Running primarily on hosted-redwood-dev with the 13B quantized candidate models (v1/v2 variants).
- Token budget: try to keep context under ~600 tokens for latency, so exemplar sets must be tiny.
- Eval is manual eyeballing for now; will feed promising templates to the eval harness later (JIRA-MLPROBE-77).

Quick templates (raw — iterate liberally):
1) Minimal anchoring + uncertainty request (EX-A):
PROMPT: You are an assistant that answers concisely. Use the facts provided, and if you're not sure, say 'I may be mistaken' and give a one-line reason.
FACTS: <short fact: e.g., 'Fermat's Last Theorem was proved by Andrew Wiles in 1994.'>
QUESTION: Did mathematician X propose a stronger conjecture in 2001?
EXPECTED: Model either says 'I may be mistaken — no record' or gives a confident hallucination to catch.

2) Contrast pair few-shot (EX-B):
Shot 1 (pos): Q: Who invented the safety valve on the steam engine? A: James Watt (patented improvements, not sole inventor) — justification: short phrase referencing improvement.
Shot 2 (neg/adversarial): Q: Who invented the safety valve on the steam engine? A: Alexander Graham Bell — clearly wrong example (labelled 'INCORRECT')
New query: Q: Who invented X? (testing whether model overgeneralizes from wrong exemplar).
Goal: See if negative exemplar causes calibration shift (worse) or helps (better discrimination).

3) Persona-anchored boundary probe (EX-C):
Single-shot: "You're an archivist. Summarize if the following claim is plausible: '<claim>' — give likelihood: high/medium/low and one evidence sentence."
This forces a role and a short confidence bucket to see whether model collapses to 'plausible' on weak evidence.

Examples and ad-hoc records (log of runs):
- 2025-11-07: v1-13b on dev. EX-A with fact about a little-known chemist. Result: model returned a confident paragraph with fabricated publication venues. Tag: hallucination-heavy.
- 2025-11-12: EX-B with contrast pair. Model tended to favor the incorrect exemplar when the negative was labelled 'INCORRECT' but not explained. Tag: negative-example framing failed (label alone not enough).
- 2026-01-09: EX-C persona-archivist. Result: model gave 'medium' plausibility but justification was circular. Tag: justification-surface, weak grounding.

Failure-mode catalog (working):
- Overconfident fabrication: model asserts precise dates/venues with zero factual tie-ins.
- Exemplar bleed: model copies details from negative exemplars when label is subtle or examples are too similar.
- Shortcutting: model gives label (plausible/unlikely) without the requested one-sentence justification.
- Truncation/format loss: streaming outputs drop the final reason if token limit near.

Quick mitigation heuristics to try (cheap first):
- Force 'uncertainty phrase' tokens: require output to start with 'I may be mistaken' or 'Uncertain:' — makes calibration explicit and easy to filter.
- Normalize negative exemplar: instead of 'INCORRECT' label alone, add 'INCORRECT — here's why: <one-sentence reason>'.
- Tiny fact-check seed: add 1–2 source markers (e.g., 'Source: Encyclopedia of X (entry)') even if fake, to test whether model latches onto source cues.
- Output schema enforcement: require response JSON with fields {"verdict":"...","support":"..."} to reduce freeform drift. (Beware: model sometimes outputs near-JSON but invalid.)

Evaluation notes / heuristics for manual triage:
- Confidence vs correctness scatter: mark outputs as (C/H) where C=claimed confidence (explicit phrase) and H=human-evaluated correctness. Watch patterns.
- Pare down exemplars: if adding a 2nd exemplar increases flakiness, revert to single-shot plus anchor.
- Track tokens-to-certainty: do longer contexts increase hallucination? Record median output length per prompt.

Concrete mini-experiments to run next (short actionable):
1) Run EX-A across v1/v2 7B/13B with and without the forced 'I may be mistaken' starter. Record 50 samples each. (Tag: JIRA-MLPROBE-77)
2) Replace 'INCORRECT' negative example with 'INCORRECT — contradiction: [explain]' and test sample set of 30 for EX-B.
3) Try output-schema enforcement for EX-C (verdict/support) and see % schema-valid responses.

Notes-to-self (style & small tips):
- Keep exemplars short (1–2 sentences) and explicit when possible.
- Use role prompts sparingly; sometimes 'assistant as archivist' reduces verbosity but can encourage hedging.
- When testing for calibration, always include a small 'gold' exemplars set to anchor evaluation.

Open questions / gamble items:
- Does a short explicit uncertainty token actually reduce hallucination or just makes the model post-hoc add the token? (A/B test needed.)
- Can a single adversarial negative example ever *help* if paired with a stronger positive exemplar? What's the ratio?
- Are there model-specific quirks (v1 vs v2) in adopting negative exemplars as 'examples to emulate' vs 'examples to avoid'?

Next steps / backlog (tiny):
- Convert successful prompts to a compact CSV with columns: id, template, exemplar_count, notes, repo_link.
- Add any high-signal prompts to the 'probe-experiments' repo as a baselined test case.
- Share a short note in #ml-probes with one interesting failure and a reproducible prompt.

Scratch snippets (raw copy-paste to experiment):
PROMPT-A: "You are an assistant. Use facts provided; if unsure, start with 'I may be mistaken' and give a one-sentence reason. Facts:
- {fact}
Question: {question}"

PROMPT-B (contrast):
Shot1: Q: Who built the first X? A: Y — [correct short justification]
Shot2: Q: Who built the first X? A: Z (INCORRECT — misattributed due to similar name)
Q: Who built the first X?

Quick record: I'm keeping this deliberately messy — notes-to-self and ephemeral test ideas belong here. When something repeats as 'signal' (good or bad), promote to the canonical probe list in the repo.

End of scratchpad.
